concept.name: Tick bar
concept.definition: A tick bar is an OHLCV bar built by aggregating a fixed number of consecutive trades (e.g., every 1,000 transactions), rather than a fixed clock interval. Sampling in transaction time aligns bar formation with market activity instead of the clock.
concept.intuition: A new bar appears after every N trades — busy markets produce bars rapidly, quiet markets slowly, so each bar contains a comparable amount of trading activity.
concept.mechanics: Count executed trades from the tick stream; every time the count reaches N, reduce those N trades to OHLCV and start a new bar. Returns sampled this way are statistically better behaved (closer to i.i.d. and normal) than time-bar returns, per López de Prado.
concept.failure_modes: Tick bars are sensitive to trade-count fragmentation: the same order flow split into more prints (by algo slicing or venue rules) produces more bars without more information, so bar frequency is not comparable across regimes or venues.
concept.misconceptions: A tick bar is not one bar per tick — it aggregates N trades, and 'tick' here means transaction, not minimum price increment.
concept.example: With 1,000-trade tick bars on ES futures, a bar may complete in seconds around the U.S. open but take minutes overnight.

citations.source: López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018)
